body.text: Pax Silica is a United States-led initiative that is presented as a victory for global supply chain resilience. Among its signatories are the Philippines and Japan. The recently unveiled project is centred around a 4,000-acre Economic Security Zone in New Clark City. The corridor seeks to link Subic Bay, Clark, Manila, and Batangas through modern facilities, clean energy grids, and high-tech manufacturing hubs. The primary objective is to position the Philippines as an indispensable node in digital infrastructure, advanced semiconductor packaging, and critical minerals.

However, beneath official diplomatic press releases, the initiative faces a wave of domestic scepticism and coordinated counter-narratives. Critics from traditional left-wing coalitions have branded the corridor as “war production disguised as development,” arguing that the New Clark City hub will compromise ancestral lands, trigger environmental degradation, and entangle Manila in a foreign military strategy. Even the Philippine President’s sister, Senator Imee Marcos, called for the initiative to be investigated. Other senators from different parties also raised concerns. Online campaigns have further amplified these concerns, alleging that high-tech manufacturing will exhaust Central Luzon’s energy supply and local water tables. These concerns are valid and deserve closer scrutiny. However, it is also worth noting that the risk of malign foreign influence, through state-backed diplomatic and media outlets, persists. Their framing of the Luzon Economic Corridor (LEC) ranges from portraying it as an aggressive containment mechanism aimed at turning the Philippines into a forward logistics base for foreign militaries and at exploiting mistrust in the government and public concern over natural resources.

The state-owned and controlled corporation, the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA), has since released statements to counteract what it considers misinformation and false assumptions. It is actively persuading the public of the benefits and potential that the LEC can bring, not only to a single region in the Philippines but to the whole country as well. In its briefing, BCDA President and CEO Joshua Bingcang pushed back on claims that the hub would drain water resources, insisting that the facility would rely on rainwater harvesting, storage, and recycling rather than on community supply, with desalination as an additional option. On the question of displacement, BCDA maintained that the site sits outside ancestral domains and that a significant share of the Clark Freeport Zone had already been set aside for Indigenous peoples well before Pax Silica was conceived. Even Imee Marcos’s more pointed allegation — that a leaked framework would grant a foreign “master tenant” 40-percent effective control over the land through a 99-year lease — was met with the same reassurance that any arrangement would remain bound by the BCDA Charter and the Investors’ Lease Act, with Bingcang describing it simply as “a business contract” that favours the host country. Despite these reassurances, a new oppositional coalition has been formed, the Network Opposed to Pax Silica. The network has noted that no Environmental Impact Assessment for the project has ever been made public, a more concrete and verifiable gap than the sovereignty debate that has dominated headlines.

Amid the criticisms and debate, there is a need to raise a fundamental policy question: Is Pax Silica truly just an exercise in foreign strategic entanglement, or could it be an essential mechanism to achieve Philippine economic and national security? Evaluating the initiative requires moving beyond ideological rhetoric and examining who benefits if the corridor fails, how regional peers are operating, and what guardrails can be implemented to ensure that Filipinos benefit from this initiative.
EVALUATING THE PAYOFFS AND TRADE-OFFS

To assess Pax Silica objectively, one must evaluate the costs of inaction. If the Luzon Economic Corridor were to stall or be cancelled, the primary beneficiaries would not be Filipino workers or local communities, but external actors with entrenched interests that profit from the status quo.

First, a derailed corridor preserves the extractive status quo for raw critical minerals. The Philippines is the world’s largest exporter of nickel ore. Under existing arrangements, raw soil is dug up domestically and shipped, mostly to China, where all high-margin refining, processing, and value addition occur. Foreign industrial hubs capture the economic rents and technical capacity, leaving the host nation with low-wage extraction jobs and local environmental fallout.

Second, rejecting the initiative guarantees that the Philippines will fall further behind its peers in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). Across the region, member states are aggressively executing targeted industrial strategies to capture global high-tech capital. They are funding infrastructure and building smoother logistics and transportation systems to attract foreign investors. Vietnam has established itself as an electronics assembly powerhouse, securing major supply chain investments from Samsung, Apple, and global semiconductor packaging firms. Malaysia has solidified its role as a premier centre for semiconductor testing and packaging, leveraging dedicated industrial hubs in Penang to attract investments in advanced microelectronics. Singapore is leading in more advanced integrated circuit (IC) design and R&D. Indonesia has transformed its domestic mining sector by placing a strict ban on unrefined nickel exports, successfully forcing foreign firms to build multi-billion-dollar domestic smelting and battery-processing infrastructure.

While the states mentioned above have already recognised that economic security is national security, without state-backed frameworks like the Luzon Economic Corridor, the Philippines remains stuck and stagnant—continuing to rely on overseas Filipino worker (OFW) remittances, sending talent abroad, and remaining in the low-value part of the technological supply chain. For citizens who demand better public goods and services, it is vital to understand that industrialization and policies like these are necessary fuel for sustainable development.
From an economic security perspective, Pax Silica cushions the Philippines against global supply shocks, arbitrary trade embargoes, and the threat of coercive economic statecraft.

In this context, industrial hubs have contributed to a better economy and quality of life for citizens of many Southeast Asian countries. Critics who advocate for rejecting Pax Silica must answer a pragmatic question: If not Pax Silica, what is the alternative? Why are they so keen on making Filipinos choose between industrialisation and human security? Is it not possible to attain both? Rejecting co-investment frameworks without offering a credible strategy to fund multi-gigawatt power grid additions, construct transportation facilities, or upgrade university engineering programmes leaves the Philippines trapped in the status quo, at the lower-value part of the supply chain in assembly, testing and packaging, with prohibitively high electricity tariffs, and raw resource exports.
FULFILLING BOTH ECONOMIC SECURITY AND NATIONAL SECURITY

The value of Pax Silica lies in an incontrovertible truth realised in the last few years: Economic security is national security, and vice versa. The two concepts, initially conceptualised as distinct areas of concern, can no longer be separated. A state that lacks energy grid stability, digital infrastructure, or the capacity to process its own natural resources cannot exercise genuine strategic autonomy. Pax Silica offers an answer.

From an economic security perspective, Pax Silica cushions the Philippines against global supply shocks, arbitrary trade embargoes, and the threat of coercive economic statecraft. By embedding domestic plants into a 24-nation trusted technology framework — including the US, Japan, South Korea, Singapore, Australia, and India — the Philippines transitions from an isolated exporter into an essential link in global high-tech manufacturing. It makes the Philippines valuable.

From a national security perspective, modern deterrence relies on economic indispensability to support requirements critical to both domestic forces and allied and security partners, rather than strictly pushing for greater military presence—another policy tension. When the Philippines hosts vital links in advanced semiconductor packaging, AI hardware, and clean energy supply chains, major regional economies acquire a direct vested interest in that nation’s territorial integrity, peace, and maritime stability. Such is the case with Taiwan. Pax Silica provides the Philippines with a multi-layered shield of mutual economic interdependence.

However, Pax Silica’s economic interdependencies have evoked criticisms and fears of being trapped in major power competition due to the many stakeholders involved. What is lost on many policymakers is that the Philippines’ political and economic proximity to major powers places Manila at the heart of this strategic competition. At this juncture, ‘rejecting’ entanglements is a difficult policy decision because it strips Manila of its economic value. It would be more prudent to ask instead how Manila ought to navigate the riptide of strategic competition that undergirds the new reality of international politics. If Manila is to navigate geopolitics and benefit from Pax Silica in the process, putting primacy on Philippine interests will be critical. This will ultimately require greater nuance in balancing, as Malaysia, Indonesia, and Singapore have done. For the Philippines to meaningfully make the most of Pax Silica, it will need to extract value in line with its national interest: shaping the industry and reform agenda, easing business regulations and processes, and setting the terms for intellectual property rights protection while allowing for technological and knowledge transfers.
THE COLD REALITY IN GEOPOLITICS
States act strictly out of self-interest; that is a given in international relations analysis. Neither the US nor China will offer multi-billion-dollar development frameworks out of altruism.

The US backs Pax Silica to maintain its technological lead and secure supply chains away from strategic chokepoints in East Asia. Japan supports the Luzon Economic Corridor to safeguard its maritime trade routes along the Bashi Channel and the South China Sea. China is warranted in viewing the initiative with scepticism because an economically resilient and integrated Philippines alters the regional balance of power.

This reality should not deter the Philippines. What it needs is strategy. On one hand, there are foreign partners (such as the Western allies) that require a stable, secure semiconductor and logistics node in Southeast Asia. On the other hand, the Philippines is well postured to serve as that important node but requires capital, technology transfer, infrastructure, and lower commercial power tariffs. Mediating between the two will fundamentally be transactional. The objective for the Philippines should be to align foreign interests first and foremost with its national industrial goals, not the other way around.

Foreign powers will only push these projects as far as they serve their strategic interests. Private industries will only invest if the math makes sense. Success or failure for the Luzon Economic Corridor rests entirely on the Philippines itself. If the Philippines operates as a passive recipient, foreign partners will shape the corridor to suit external priorities. If the country operates as an assertive, self-interested negotiator, it can leverage international competition to build permanent and strategic domestic industrial capability.
IMPLEMENTING PAX SILICA RIGHT

Pax Silica represents a wise choice for the Philippines—if done right. The criticism surrounding the initiative should not cause Manila to retreat or surrender to policy paralysis. Instead, it should push Philippine leaders to execute the initiative with ruthless, pragmatic focus. To ensure the Luzon Economic Corridor fulfils its potential and delivers tangible benefits to the Filipino people, Manila should implement key policy directives.

First, the Philippines must learn from Indonesia and leverage its critical mineral reserves by requiring local mineral processing. Foreign firms operating inside the New Clark City Economic Security Zone must be required to form joint ventures with domestic entities to construct local refining and packaging facilities, with raw ore exports systematically phased out.

Second, learning from its past, Manila should maintain open access and regulatory sovereignty. Given that Pax Silica is a multilateral initiative, the Bases Conversion and Development Authority must ensure that logistics corridors, ports, and industrial zones remain under Philippine regulatory authority and open to non-US commercial tenants. Preserving open access protects national flexibility and prevents industrial zones from becoming single-partner enclaves.

Third, the government must ensure that the country is ready for investments, and address local impacts. It must allay fears of environmental damage through transparency, and deliver comprehensive infrastructure plans. It is non-negotiable that an unbiased Environmental Impact Assessment be conducted. Equally essential are consultations with affected Indigenous peoples and transparency in official plans, especially those that concern water and power sources, including BCDA’s rainwater harvesting and industrial recycling systems. Safeguards and thresholds must be strictly enforced. If data centres do not make sense, then the government should select investors who will build better Philippine technologies, whether it be advanced IC design, assembly, testing, and packaging (ATP), or even wafer fabs and foundries. They bring technology transfer and high-skilled employment. Investment funds should directly support, if not sustain, local power grid upgrades, technical-vocational programmes, and municipal infrastructure, ensuring surrounding communities realise tangible economic benefits. Listening to public opinion remains vital, especially since it is the citizens who will suffer the negative consequences if anything goes amiss.

Finally, securing a sustainable energy future is paramount. With the Malampaya gas field projected to deplete by 2027, the Philippines must urgently diversify its power generation to support the high energy demands of the Luzon Economic Corridor. Pax Silica provides the framework to scale up geothermal power, solar and other renewable energy, and to explore nuclear feasibility. Integrating these energy sources is essential to ensure that the Economic Security Zone remains energy-secure and competitive in the long term. This model can later be studied for replication in the rest of the country.
CONCLUSION

The Pax Silica policy is a test of Philippine strategic clarity. Criticisms regarding environmental impact, sovereignty, and foreign entanglement are warranted and deserve rigorous oversight, but rejecting the initiative out of fear and propaganda offers no path to securing a place in the supply chain or achieving industrialisation. Choosing between Pax Silica and other public goods is a false dichotomy, and rejecting the initiative altogether neglects the bigger picture.

Geopolitics is inherently self-interested. The US will not build the Philippines’ industrial base, at least not without alignment of interests. Small states have agency and do not have to function as passive actors in major power competition. With an honest and strategic government, paired with a vibrant and watchful civil society, the Philippines can facilitate and navigate it — and still win in the process. Pax Silica is not an initiative of the US alone, and the Philippines has much to gain from utilising this network. By recognising who benefits from the status quo, evaluating regional realities, and maintaining a firm position at the negotiating table, the Philippines can leverage Pax Silica to advance its economic and national security interests. Executed correctly, the Luzon Economic Corridor presents huge potential. It can serve not only as an important tool for navigating between foreign powers but also as a foundation for long-term Philippine economic security.
